Minimum Risk Point Estimation of a Normal Mean

Source: R/seq_mr_norm_mean.R
seq_mr_norm_mean.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) procedure for the mean of a normal population with unknown variance (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009, Section 6.4, who credit the original formulation to Robbins, 1959). Estimation error and sampling both cost something; the procedure looks for the sample size at which their expected total, the risk, is smallest. That sample size depends on the unknown variance, so observations are collected until the sample size reaches the size the current variance estimate calls for. The procedure is risk based, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

seq_mr_norm_mean(x, A = NULL, c, price = NULL, epsilon = NULL, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 2).

A

The loss constant: the price of one unit of squared estimation error, in the same currency as c. A positive number. Either supply A directly, or supply price and epsilon, in which case \(A = \mathrm{price}/\mathrm{epsilon}^2\).

c

The cost of sampling one observation. A positive number.

price, epsilon

An alternative way to state A (Chattopadhyay and Kelley, 2016): price is the amount one is willing to pay for an estimate within epsilon of the mean, and \(A = \mathrm{price}/\mathrm{epsilon}^2\). Both positive numbers; supply both or neither.

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

mean

The sample mean, the point estimate.

risk

The estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A S_n^2/n + c\,n\).

optimal_n

The sample size the current estimate of the standard deviation calls for, \(\lceil (A/c)^{1/2} S_n \rceil\).

current_n

The number of observations used.

risk and optimal_n are NA when the data are constant. Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE when current_n has reached optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), method, loss_A, cost_c, variance_unusable (TRUE when the data are constant, so that no variance has been estimated), and notes. conf_level and width are NULL.

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_mr_norm_mean_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

The loss from estimating the mean \(\mu\) by the sample mean of \(n\) observations is $$L_n = A(\bar{X}_n - \mu)^2 + c\,n$$ (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009, Equation 6.4.1): \(A\) prices a unit of squared estimation error and \(c\) is the cost of one observation. Its expectation for a fixed \(n\), the risk, is \(A\sigma^2/n + c\,n\) (their Equation 6.4.2), which is smallest at \(n^* = (A/c)^{1/2}\sigma\) (their Equation 6.4.3), where it equals \(2 c\,n^*\). The sequential rule replaces \(\sigma\) by the sample standard deviation \(S_n\): sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) with $$n \ge (A/c)^{1/2} S_n .$$ The optimal_n row is the right hand side rounded up, and the risk row is the estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A S_n^2/n + c\,n\); both are evaluated at the current data.

The optimality is asymptotic. As the cost per observation falls (so that \(n^*\) grows), the expected final sample size approaches \(n^*\) and the risk of the procedure approaches the minimum \(2 c\,n^*\). When \(n^*\) is small the procedure sometimes stops early on an underestimate of the standard deviation, and its risk is somewhat above the minimum. In simulation (normal data, the pilot of seq_mr_norm_mean_pilot() with its defaults, 40,000 replications, Monte Carlo standard error at most 0.005), with a standard deviation of 1 the ratio of the risk to the minimum was 1.07, 1.06, 1.04, 1.01, and 1.00 when \(n^*\) was 10, 15, 20, 50, and 100 (that is, when \(A/c\) was 100, 225, 400, 2,500, and 10,000, for which the pilot is 4, 4, 5, 8, and 10). The ratio is not a function of \(n^*\) alone: the pilot depends only on \(A/c\), so the same \(n^*\) reached with another standard deviation starts from a different pilot. With a standard deviation of 0.25 (pilots of 7 to 20) the five ratios were 1.02, 1.03, 1.02, 1.01, and 1.00, and with a standard deviation of 4 (pilots of 4 or 5) they were 1.07, 1.07, 1.04, 1.00, and 1.00.

Constant data. If every observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value, as with gain scores of 0.3 computed as posttest minus pretest), the standard deviation estimate is zero, or nothing but rounding error, and the rule as printed would be met at once. The function departs from the printed rule deliberately: no variance has been estimated, so the rule is reported as not met, risk and optimal_n are NA, attr(out, "variance_unusable") is TRUE, and a note says so (see smsd_check_methods); data whose real spread is that small beside their size should have a common value subtracted first.

Extreme units. Data that do vary, but whose spread is so large or so small that the sample variance cannot be represented in double precision (differences among the observations beyond about \(10^{154}\) or below about \(10^{-162}\)), are an error that says to change the units. That case is not reported as a rule not yet met, because collecting more data cannot help.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

Robbins, H. (1959). Sequential estimation of the mean of a normal population. In U. Grenander (Ed.), Probability and statistics: The Harald Cramer volume (pp. 235–245). Almqvist & Wiksell.

See also

seq_mr_norm_mean_pilot for the pilot. With no normality assumption: seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb. To bound the risk of the same kind of loss instead of trading it against cost: seq_br_norm_mean.

Other seq_mr_norm_mean: seq_mr_norm_mean_pilot()

Author

Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in, Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# A school district wants its mean test score. An error of one point
# (squared) is valued at 2,500 dollars and testing one more student
# costs 4 dollars. Scores are simulated here with a standard deviation
# of 12, so the best sample size is sqrt(2500 / 4) * 12 = 300.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_mr_norm_mean_pilot(A = 2500, c = 4)
scores <- rnorm(m, mean = 70, sd = 12)
out <- seq_mr_norm_mean(scores, A = 2500, c = 4)
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 5
#>   Criterion n     : 316
#> 
#>   mean              : 70.97121
#>   risk              : 79636.06
#>   optimal_n         : 316
#>   current_n         : 5
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one student at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  scores <- c(scores, rnorm(1, mean = 70, sd = 12))
  out <- seq_mr_norm_mean(scores, A = 2500, c = 4)
}
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 299
#>   Criterion n     : 299
#> 
#>   mean              : 69.45986
#>   risk              : 2386.488
#>   optimal_n         : 299
#>   current_n         : 299
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
